title: Measuring AGI: Interactive Reasoning Benchmarks for ARC-AGI-3 — Greg Kamradt, ARC Prize Foundation

summary: Greg Kamradt, President of ARC Prize Foundation (a nonprofit founded by François Chollet and Mike Knoop), presents the case for interactive reasoning benchmarks as the next evolution in measuring AGI. The talk opens with popular agent demos (Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini playing Pokémon) to illustrate that current agents, while impressive, get stuck for days, hallucinate actions, and rely on Pokémon training data already within the model rather than genuine novel reasoning. ARC's opinionated approach targets humans as the benchmark for general intelligence, since humans are the sole known proof point. Kamradt cites two definitions of intelligence: John McCarthy's (machines doing tasks they've never seen or prepared for) and Chollet's (skill acquisition efficiency). ARC-AGI v1 tested learning a mini-skill from input-output grid transformations and demonstrating it on a test grid. ARC-AGI v2 contains over 1,000 novel tasks where no skill repeats across tasks; the team tested 400+ people in San Diego to verify every task is human-solvable. However, single-turn benchmarks miss interactive intelligence—exploring open worlds, understanding goals, and acting on sparse rewards. This aligns with Rich Sutton's 'Welcome to the Era of Experience' paper. Games are proposed as the ideal medium: complex rules, defined scope, and flexibility. Previous Atari benchmarks suffered from dense rewards, irregular reporting, no hidden test sets, and developer knowledge leakage. ARC-AGI-3, launching Q1 2026 with ~120 games, is ARC's first interactive reasoning benchmark, featuring a public training set and a private evaluation set with no internet access, forcing understanding through exploration without instructions. The benchmark restricts tasks to four core knowledge priors only—basic math, basic geometry, agentness (theory of mind), and objectness—stripping away language, symbols, and trivia to test the reliability floor rather than superhuman specialization. Evaluation uses skill acquisition efficiency: hundreds of humans will be tested to establish baselines for time and action count, and AI will be measured the same way. Kamradt asserts that if AI cannot match human performance on these tasks, AGI has not been achieved. A sandbox preview of five games and a mini agent competition with prize money is planned for the following month in San Francisco. The team abandoned Unity for a lightweight custom Python engine and is recruiting game developers, adversarial testers, and donors. In Q&A, Kamradt estimates the benchmark will take years (not decades) to saturate, explains that ideal efficiency denominators would be energy and training data but proxies like cost and action count are used in turn-based games, defines objectness as recognizing pixels moving together as one body, and notes that tasks humans cannot do are out of scope as they pertain to superintelligence rather than AGI measurement.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Opening Demos and Agent Limitations
sections.summary: Kamradt opens with popular agent demos—Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini playing Pokémon—to show that while impressive, these agents get stuck for days, hallucinate actions, and rely on Pokémon training data already in the model, rather than demonstrating genuine novel reasoning.

sections.title: ARC Prize Foundation and Human-Targeted Approach
sections.summary: Kamradt introduces ARC as a nonprofit founded by François Chollet and Mike Knoop, invited by OpenAI to co-announce o3 results on ARC-AGI. ARC's opinionated approach targets humans as the benchmark for general intelligence, creating a measurable gap between human and AI capabilities that also guides research.

sections.title: Defining General Intelligence
sections.summary: Two definitions of intelligence are cited: McCarthy's (machines doing tasks they've never seen or prepared for) and Chollet's (skill acquisition efficiency). Memorization of seen problems is contrasted with genuine on-the-fly learning.

sections.title: ARC-AGI v1 and v2 Benchmarks
sections.summary: ARC-AGI v1 tests learning a mini-skill from input-output grid transformations and demonstrating it. ARC-AGI v2 has over 1,000 novel tasks where each skill is unique. ARC tested 400+ people in San Diego to verify every task is human-solvable.

sections.title: Need for Interactive Reasoning Benchmarks
sections.summary: Single-turn benchmarks miss interactive intelligence: exploring open worlds, understanding goals, and acting on sparse rewards. This aligns with Rich Sutton's 'Welcome to the Era of Experience' paper calling for agents that engage with open worlds and build their own world models.

sections.title: Games as Medium and Atari Limitations
sections.summary: Games are proposed as ideal for interactive benchmarks due to complex rules, defined scope, and flexibility. Previous Atari benchmarks failed due to dense rewards, irregular reporting, no hidden test sets, and developers injecting their own game knowledge into models. The target assertion is AI beating 100 unseen games that neither the system nor developer has encountered.

sections.title: ARC-AGI-3 Sneak Preview
sections.summary: ARC-AGI-3 is announced as ARC's first interactive reasoning benchmark, launching Q1 2026. It features ~40 public training games and a private evaluation set with no internet access, unseen by both AI and developers. It forces understanding through exploration without instructions, exemplified by the 'Locksmith' game.

sections.title: Core Knowledge Priors and Design Principles
sections.summary: Kamradt explains ARC-AGI-3 requires only core knowledge priors, carried from v1 and v2: no language, symbols, or trivia. Rather than chasing superhuman 'PhD plus++' problems, ARC focuses on the reliability floor. The four priors are basic math, basic geometry, agentness (theory of mind), and objectness—cognitive primitives humans are born with or acquire immediately after birth.

sections.title: Evaluation Methodology: Skill Acquisition Efficiency
sections.summary: Evaluation returns to Chollet's skill acquisition efficiency definition. Hundreds of humans will be tested on ARC-AGI-3 tasks to measure time and action count, establishing a baseline. AI is measured the same way. Kamradt asserts that if AI cannot match humans on tasks humans can do, AGI has not been achieved.

sections.title: Sandbox Preview, Roadmap, and Call for Participation
sections.summary: A sandbox preview of 5 games is planned for next month in San Francisco with a mini agent competition and prize money. The full target is ~120 games by Q1 2026. Each game is rich with multiple levels. ARC abandoned Unity for a lightweight custom Python engine. Kamradt calls for donations, adversarial testers, and game developers/designers.

sections.title: Q&A: Saturation Timeline, Efficiency, Objectness, and Scope
sections.summary: Kamradt estimates benchmark saturation in years, not decades. Ideal efficiency denominators would be energy (calories of human brain) and training data, but closed models make these inaccessible; proxies are cost and action count. Games are turn-based with no wall-clock timing. Objectness is defined as recognizing pixels moving together as one body. Tasks humans cannot do are out of scope, as they pertain to superintelligence rather than AGI measurement.
